paras: The assault on John Logan was an attack by three white men on John Logan, a Black hotel bellboy, on South Meridian street in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of April 28, 1903. It drew notice because Logan said two patrolmen had used him as a decoy against the "bungaloo" rowdies and then left him, a charge that led the mayor to order an inquiry.
The Indianapolis Journal described the "bungaloos" as rowdies "who take delight in overpowering negroes and beating them."

Riding his bicycle around Monument place about 9 o'clock, Logan was called "nigger" and threatened by several drunken white men. Patrolmen Dolby and Gregory searched with him without result. By Logan's first account, the officers had him wait outside the Postal Telegraph office to lure the men toward Pearl street, where they would make arrests. When the men came, one struck him in the mouth and another knocked him down, and the patrolmen were gone; one also punctured his bicycle. His cut lip took three stitches at the City Dispensary, and the police could not find the assailants.

On April 29 Mayor Bookwalter directed the Board of Public Safety to investigate whether the patrolmen had used Logan as a decoy and failed to protect him. He said the "bungaloo business must be broken up," and an extra force was assigned to South Illinois street. No report of the board's finding or of any arrest appears in the coverage.

The Journal broke the story under "COLORED BELL BOY ATTACKED AND CRUELLY BEATEN," saying the policemen had left Logan "a victim to the three men." A day later it reported the inquiry under "AFTER BUNGALOO GANG" but added an item, "DID NOT NEGLECT DUTY," calling its earlier impression of the patrolmen "erroneous." The German-language Indiana Tribüne noted only the mayor's order; no Black-press report appears in the coverage.

The police-side account, which Logan later endorsed in a written statement, held that the patrolmen spent an hour and twenty minutes with him, advised him to go home and left, and that he was struck but not knocked down.

reader.title: Assault on John Logan
bases: Three white men identified as members of the 'bungaloo' rowdies struck Logan, a Black bellboy, in the street and punctured his bicycle; no killing and no official perpetrators (A1, A3).

Only The Indianapolis Journal reports the assault itself, in two articles that agree on the attack but differ on details and on the police's conduct (A1, A3); the Indiana Tribüne confirms only the ensuing inquiry (A4).

accounts.label: Logan's first account
accounts.gist: The patrolmen told him to wait outside the Postal Telegraph office and lure the men to Pearl street, promising to arrest them there; when the men came, one hit him in the mouth and another knocked him down, and the policemen had gone.

accounts.label: Police version
accounts.gist: The patrolmen spent an hour and twenty minutes searching with Logan, waited at Pearl and Meridian streets, then agreed the men would not return and advised him to go home; the men came back after the officers left, struck him once without knocking him down, and punctured his bicycle.

accounts.label: Logan's later statement
accounts.gist: Logan gave the police a written statement that they had been with him an hour and twenty minutes and said at the station it was not their fault he was beaten.

framing.detail: The Journal's first headline, 'COLORED BELL BOY ATTACKED AND CRUELLY BEATEN', and its deck, 'Attack Made in Pure Maliciousness', faulted the assailants and pictured the police leaving Logan 'a victim'.
Next day the Journal reported the mayor's inquiry under 'AFTER BUNGALOO GANG' but added 'DID NOT NEGLECT DUTY', calling its own earlier impression 'erroneous' on the police's word.
The German-language Indiana Tribüne reported only the mayor's order under 'Krieg den Bungaloos', without naming Logan.
